Unlike obesity in adults, obesity in children is defined relative to other children (i.e. being above a certain BMI percentile for a child's specific age and sex group). This puts a ceiling on the percentage of children that are defined as obese, even if children are getting fatter as a group. At least, that's my understanding based on this: https://www.cdc.gov/obesity/childhood/defining.html.

There is probably something to that. However, in my understanding: childhood BMI guidelines are defined relative to a reference population, though this is not the current population. In the UK the British 1990 growth reference (UK90) is recommended. http://www.noo.org.uk/uploads/doc/vid_11601_A_simple_guide_to_classifying_BMI_in_children.pdf

It would be difficult to determine exact guidelines, since population is changing in a variety of ways (e.g. earlier onset of puberty, people are getting taller etc) - so it wouldn't be easy to come up with an "ideal" healthy growth reference. (E.g. a UK33 would probably not be suitable.) However, I would hope that the reference is not that bad that we'd translate a rate of 30% overweight for children into 70% overweight for adults. Also, it strikes me as likely that people gain weight over time, so teenagers at a healthy weight and bad eating habits will eventually grow into adults with an unhealthy weight and bad eating habits.
